prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and its experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I opened with the Higgs observation, but the opening ballots show that topological insulators are the one candidate that almost everyone ranks highly and for scientific reasons rather than habit: seven of eight members place B039 in their lists, four in the top three. It is a clear case of the discovery-first principle. Kane and Mele identified a new organising principle, a Z2 invariant that protects edge and surface states, and Molenkamp's group then found the clue in nature, quantised edge conduction in HgTe wells, so the idea was tested rather than merely admired. The concept has since travelled into 3D materials, photonics and cold atoms. Confirmation is independent and long-standing, and the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions did not cover this body of work, so the recognition is mature and not premature. The prediction-then-observation structure also gives a defensible three-person split, which is something B028 and B003 cannot offer.
statement.case_against: The credited trio is not the whole story. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe as the host and made the experiment possible, Fu, Kane and Mele together with Moore and Balents opened the 3D case, and Hasan's ARPES work established the first 3D materials. Zhang has died, which simplifies one issue and sharpens another. A three-person limit forces us to choose between honouring the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and honouring topological insulators as a whole, and the citation wording has to carry that choice. Partial overlap with the 2016 prize is a further reservation, as is the fact that much of the practical impact is still conceptual. If the committee thinks the allocation cannot be defended, B022 is the cleaner two-name case.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the Higgs observation sixth. He holds that the theory was honoured in 2013, that the credited names are leadership-based, and that this clashes with the tradition of rewarding specific individual contributions.
responses.response: This is a fair challenge and I now concede more of it than I did in my opening. The physics is exceptional, but I cannot show that Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee are the decisive individual contributors, and the opening support for B028 is only two members. I still think the observation is a real gap, because the 2013 prize honoured a 1964 mechanism and not the 2012 evidence, and I would not drop it altogether. But a prize that is contested on attribution at the moment of choosing is weaker than one where theory and experiment map onto named people. I therefore move B028 to an alternative. I also disagree with Pearce on one point: his reservations about B049 on the same grounds (other optical teams, the theorists) apply almost equally to B028, so we should hold both to the same standard.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first and argues it is a textbook case of a measurement technique that moves the limit of what can be observed, with clean two-name attribution and independent confirmation.
responses.response: I take the attribution argument seriously. Katori and Ye are the cleanest pair on the list, and the 10^-18 results are as solid as anything we have. Where I differ is on ranking it above topological insulators. The comb prize in 2005 and the 2012 prize for controlling single ions both address the toolbox on which the clocks rest, and the redefinition of the second has not happened, so the culminating application is still pending. A clock is a superb measurement; it does not yet show nature doing something unexpected. I would not oppose B022 and I keep it as my first alternative, but I want Kroll and the other clock supporters to say what new fact about the world a lattice clock has already delivered, beyond a smaller error bar.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first, with a clear theory-experiment loop, and he acknowledges that omitting Bernevig, Zhang, Hasan and Moore makes allocation contestable and rests on memory for the priority history.
responses.response: I agree on the loop and on the stable interpretation. I would push him on the allocation: the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal is what turned Molenkamp's measurement from a hope into a test, so the citation should not read as if Kane and Mele alone predicted what was observed. I suggest the citation names the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators in two dimensions and does not claim the whole 3D field. That makes the trio defensible, and the BHZ and Hasan contributions can be handled by the Secretary's external-expert requests before round 2. I also want him to say whether he thinks the 3D case is a separate achievement or part of the same one.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, argues it underlies essentially all superconducting processors, and flags his own proximity to that community as a possible reason for recusal.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour about the conflict, and I suggest it be recorded properly. On the merits, I am not persuaded that B023 should lead. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, and Lindroth and Olsson both place cQED seventh for that reason; awarding the closely adjacent architecture straight after looks like a repeated field. Girvin's role in the 2004 proposal is also unresolved within the credited names. I would revisit it in a few years, when the distinction between the 2025 physics and the cQED architecture is easier to defend.

uncertainties: Whether Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, or the 3D topological insulator pioneers, must be included for the prize to be fair, and whether the three-person limit permits it.
How much weight to give the 2016 topological phase-transition prize when the committee judges novelty.
Whether the committee will accept leadership-based credit for ATLAS and CMS at all; if not, B028 cannot be revived.
Which of B022 and B039 the external experts regard as more decisive; I am relying on memory for priority details.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile with any shortlisted candidate or credited name. My supervisor David Gross, my co-author Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala string group are not connected to any shortlisted ballot. Topological insulators are outside my own field, so I defer partly to the condensed-matter members on priority.
